synthesis.draft:
# Architecture, Data, and Task Fit: Comparing the Original Vision Transformer with CNN Backbones

## Abstract

This review uses a mechanism-to-evidence frame to compare the original convolution-free ViT with conventional CNN backbones, while separating later pyramid, pooled and hybrid Transformers from plain ViT. ViT applies self-attention directly to fixed patch tokens and can aggregate global information early; after large-scale pretraining it matched or exceeded strong convolutional networks on ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and related transfer benchmarks under the original paper's conditions. CNNs instead build local, hierarchical feature maps through staged convolution and downsampling, giving them a natural interface for detection and segmentation heads. CKA evidence also shows measurably different internal organization: ViT layers are more uniform, with strong residual propagation, whereas ResNet representations divide more clearly into stages. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:01e8a4dbfcbc] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:7f5d1d9565aa] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:d61b3a2c0154] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:5e2261452395] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:b62e6b456bd6] [E:arxiv:2103.16302:abstract:claim:52d2ac897ca9] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:0:f6930946851d:claim:fd8c2f06a84a] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:83a29ddc89e9] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:229fa6f9a60c] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:2a4fef07e3b5] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:d69956438fbf] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:055b01c7c4c7]

The evidence does not support a task-independent winner. In broad pretrained-backbone benchmarking, Battle of the Backbones found supervised convolutional networks best on most tasks in the tested set, but tied this pattern partly to larger supervised pretraining datasets and reported ViTs to be more sensitive to pretraining-data amount and parameter count. For dense prediction, matched PVT–RetinaNet results on COCO favored pyramid Transformers over ResNet/ResNeXt backbones, while the reported single-scale ViT-S/32 was weak in that interface; this supports hierarchy and dense-feature design rather than an unchanged-ViT advantage. Efficiency is similarly conditional: token count, resolution, memory, latency, hardware and pretraining must be assessed separately from accuracy. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:1:452441575086:claim:ea0c6a09db7a] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:2754995a3368] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:b62e6b456bd6] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:5e2261452395] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:e107f162ef5e] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:7f5d1d9565aa] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:1381ace2c5eb] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:01e8a4dbfcbc] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:a04e8d78ee90] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:e9de05afa6a2] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:3b258dca8f46] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:359b663e5dc3] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:574bddc5a23a] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:0:f6930946851d:claim:fd8c2f06a84a]

## Introduction

This review compares the original Vision Transformer (ViT) with convolutional neural-network backbones used as computer-vision feature extractors. The organizing choice is a mechanism-to-evidence comparison: first separate how plain ViT and CNN backbones build visual features, then compare them under matched tasks, pretraining data, model scale, and downstream heads. This grouping is an analytical frame for the review rather than a universal taxonomy or a classification asserted by any single paper. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:01e8a4dbfcbc] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:7f5d1d9565aa]

ViT's defining departure was to remove the requirement for a convolutional backbone: an image is split into fixed patch tokens, and standard Transformer blocks with self-attention and feed-forward layers operate directly on that sequence. The original paper reported that, after large-scale pretraining and transfer to ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and other recognition benchmarks, ViT matched or exceeded strong convolutional networks while using substantially fewer training computational resources. That claim is therefore conditional on large-data pretraining and transfer, not on random initialization or small-data training alone. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:01e8a4dbfcbc] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:d61b3a2c0154]

Convolutional backbones instead construct features through local filters, hierarchical stages, increasing receptive fields, and progressively reduced spatial resolutions. This inductive design became the default backbone pattern for classification and dense prediction, but it is not identical to every later model: hybrid or convolution-infused Transformers, pyramid Transformers, and modern ConvNeXt-style networks deliberately borrow across the two families. Consequently, comparisons should distinguish the original plain ViT from later hierarchical or CNN-fused variants rather than treating all Transformers as one architecture. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:5e2261452395] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:b62e6b456bd6] [E:arxiv:2103.16302:abstract:claim:52d2ac897ca9] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:0:f6930946851d:claim:fd8c2f06a84a]

The comparison also depends on the objective. Image classification can use ViT's single-scale patch-token representation, whereas detection and segmentation commonly require dense, multi-scale feature maps; PVT and ViT-CoMer explicitly identify plain ViT's limited output scales and weak local feature interaction as dense-prediction weaknesses. Efficiency is another separate dimension: attention can aggregate global context early, but token count, resolution, latency, memory, hardware and pretraining availability change the trade-off. Later chapters therefore keep classification accuracy, dense-prediction fit, representation behavior, and deployment efficiency as distinct comparison dimensions. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:229fa6f9a60c] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:b62e6b456bd6] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:c41bdf05bdc3] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:80b3379c43b9] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:0aecb65d2202] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:29e8b5535db7]

## Background and Method Taxonomy

For this review, the taxonomy is organized by four comparison criteria rather than by publication date: feature-construction mechanism, feature hierarchy, target task interface, and efficiency/deployment constraints. The first asks whether a backbone builds representations mainly through local convolution and depth, through global self-attention over patch tokens, or through an explicit mixture. The second asks whether it preserves one token-resolution map or produces a hierarchy of scales. The third asks whether its outputs fit classification heads directly or can be inserted into dense-prediction frameworks. The fourth separates accuracy from token count, resolution, memory, latency and hardware behavior. These are review criteria for comparing the original ViT with CNN backbones; they are not presented as a universal architecture taxonomy. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:01e8a4dbfcbc] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:5e2261452395] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:b62e6b456bd6] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:0aecb65d2202]

At the mechanism end of this grouping, the original ViT is the convolution-free endpoint: fixed image patches become tokens, and repeated Transformer blocks model relations across the sequence. A conventional CNN backbone is the local-processing endpoint: convolutional filters operate on neighboring spatial locations, with depth and staged downsampling enlarging the effective receptive field. Hybrid designs should not be collapsed into either endpoint. CvT introduces convolutional token embedding and convolutional projections into a Transformer, while ViT-CoMer keeps a plain ViT branch but adds a CNN branch with multi-receptive-field features and bidirectional fusion. Their evidence therefore concerns a mixed mechanism, not the unchanged original ViT. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:01e8a4dbfcbc] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:0:f6930946851d:claim:fd8c2f06a84a] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:c41bdf05bdc3] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:80b3379c43b9] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:0aecb65d2202]

The hierarchy criterion distinguishes architecture from operator type. A standard CNN backbone naturally has stagewise feature maps with decreasing spatial resolution and increasing channels, which is why PiT and HVT describe pooling or token downsampling as borrowing a CNN-like spatial-dimension-reduction principle. The original ViT instead processes a generally uniform patch sequence and is commonly characterized as lacking the multi-scale feature hierarchy useful for dense prediction. PVT addresses this by building a progressive shrinking pyramid while remaining a Transformer, showing that “Transformer” does not necessarily imply “single-scale,” just as a modern hybrid need not be classified as a conventional CNN merely because it contains convolution. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:5e2261452395] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:b62e6b456bd6] [E:arxiv:2103.16302:abstract:claim:52d2ac897ca9] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:29e8b5535db7]

The task-interface criterion separates classification backbones from backbones intended as drop-in replacements in detection and segmentation pipelines. The original ViT was aimed at image classification and transfer to recognition benchmarks; its low-resolution, single-scale token representation is not the same interface as the hierarchical feature maps expected by frameworks such as RetinaNet or Mask R-CNN. PVT explicitly motivates its pyramid as a way to plug into these dense-prediction pipelines, and ViT-CoMer similarly targets weak local interaction and limited scale diversity in plain ViT for detection, instance segmentation and semantic segmentation. Thus, a classification result should not be read as direct evidence of dense-prediction suitability when the output interface differs. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:01e8a4dbfcbc] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:5e2261452395] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:b62e6b456bd6] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:c41bdf05bdc3] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:80b3379c43b9]

Efficiency is a related but separate axis and should not be inferred from architecture name alone. Self-attention can provide early global aggregation, but its cost depends on token count and input resolution; CNNs also vary widely by width, depth, downsampling and hardware. LeViT is classified here as a fast-inference hybrid because it combines attention with CNN-inspired decreasing activation-map resolutions and reports speed/accuracy trade-offs across hardware, whereas HVT reduces cost by progressively pooling tokens. These designs address inference efficiency, which is different from improving representation hierarchy, dense-prediction compatibility, or accuracy under a fixed pretraining corpus. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:a04e8d78ee90] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:abstract:claim:c935a9a2dd19] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:29e8b5535db7]

Finally, the taxonomy separates architectural behavior from pretraining and benchmark regime. The CKA analysis places ViTs and ResNets in different representation-structure groups: ViTs exhibit more uniform representations across layers, early global information aggregation and strong residual propagation from lower to higher layers, whereas ResNet representations divide more clearly into stages. Battle of the Backbones adds another dimension—initialization and pretraining source—by benchmarking supervised, self-supervised, vision-language and other pretrained backbones across many tasks. Consequently, a fair comparison must state whether models share parameter scale, resolution, task head, pretraining dataset and supervision; otherwise “CNN versus ViT” is not a single controlled comparison. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:229fa6f9a60c] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:7f5d1d9565aa] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:1381ace2c5eb] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:2a4fef07e3b5] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:d69956438fbf]

## Representative Methods

The original ViT is best understood as a sequence model rather than a staged feature pyramid. Its input pipeline divides an image into fixed-size, non-overlapping patches, linearly embeds those patches, adds positional information, and passes the resulting tokens through standard Transformer blocks. Each block uses multi-head self-attention to mix information across patch locations and a position-wise feed-forward network to transform each token; residual connections and normalization preserve and propagate token features through depth. The central contribution was empirical: a pure Transformer applied directly to image patches did not need a CNN encoder, and after large-scale pretraining it transferred strongly to ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and other recognition benchmarks. Its applicability boundary is therefore important: the original evidence establishes a convolution-free classification and transfer backbone under large-data pretraining, not a claim that the same unmodified token interface is optimal for every dense-prediction or low-data setting. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:01e8a4dbfcbc] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:d61b3a2c0154] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:83a29ddc89e9]

The mechanism that most distinguishes plain ViT from a conventional CNN is the spatial scope of feature mixing. Self-attention computes interactions among tokens from the beginning of the network, so information from distant image regions can be aggregated in early layers rather than waiting for repeated local convolution and downsampling to enlarge the receptive field. A representation-analysis study using centered kernel alignment found that ViTs had a much more uniform layer-similarity structure than ResNets, whose representations separated more clearly into lower and higher stages. The same analysis attributed key parts of this difference to self-attention enabling early global aggregation and to ViT residual connections strongly propagating lower-layer features into higher layers. These findings describe how ViT represents images; they do not by themselves establish higher task accuracy, because representation structure, accuracy and downstream compatibility are different criteria. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:229fa6f9a60c] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:2a4fef07e3b5] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:d69956438fbf]

Conventional CNN backbones use a different inductive bias. Convolution applies learned local filters over neighboring pixels or feature-map locations, and stacking layers increases the effective receptive field. Typical classification and detection backbones organize these operations into stages that reduce spatial resolution while increasing channel width, yielding a hierarchy of local-to-global feature maps. This design encodes locality, translation sharing and staged scale directly into the architecture. Its contribution was not merely historical: CNNs remained strong practical backbones because their feature maps fit established detection and segmentation heads and because large supervised-pretraining regimes could produce broadly transferable features. Thus, the relevant comparison is not “global attention always beats local convolution,” but whether global token mixing, hierarchical locality, pretraining and the target head are well matched. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:5e2261452395] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:b62e6b456bd6] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:7f5d1d9565aa]

ResNet is the clearest reference point for the CNN backbone family in this comparison. Its repeated residual blocks process local feature maps, and deeper variants stack more blocks or use wider grouped forms to increase capacity. In the CKA study, ResNet layers formed more stage-like representation regions than ViT, and cross-model comparisons showed that many lower ResNet layers were needed to become similar to the lower portion of a ViT. This is consistent with the architectural distinction: ResNet generally builds global context progressively through local operations, whereas ViT can access the full token set at each attention layer. However, ResNet should not stand for every CNN: later convolutional designs changed training, normalization, depth, width and stage design, so results for ResNet do not automatically generalize to modern ConvNeXt-class models. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:229fa6f9a60c] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:2a4fef07e3b5] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:d69956438fbf] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:7f5d1d9565aa]

Modern convolutional backbones complicate any simple “ViT versus CNN” ranking. Battle of the Backbones benchmarked a broad set of pretrained architectures and initialization recipes across classification, detection, out-of-distribution generalization and other tasks using more than 1,500 training runs. Its reported top performers included supervised ConvNeXt-Base, SwinV2-Base trained with ImageNet-21k, and CLIP ViT-Base, while ConvNeXt-Tiny and SwinV2-Tiny were strong at smaller scale. The study also reported that supervised convolutional networks performed best on most tasks among the models considered, while noting that the advantage was often tied to larger supervised pretraining datasets and that self-supervised models were competitive in dataset-scale-matched comparisons. This evidence supports a conditional conclusion about available pretrained backbones, not an intrinsic and task-independent superiority of convolution. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:7f5d1d9565aa] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:1381ace2c5eb]

The original ViT also has a scale-and-data boundary that should be kept separate from its architecture. ViT's strongest results depended on large pretraining corpora such as ImageNet-22k or JFT-300M before transfer to smaller or medium-sized benchmarks; the original paper framed its excellent results relative to convolutional networks in that large-scale pretraining regime. Battle of the Backbones similarly reported that ViTs were more sensitive than CNNs to the amount of pretraining data and number of parameters. This means a ViT trained from scratch on a small dataset is not being evaluated under the premise that made the original model competitive. Conversely, a CNN's strong result after large supervised pretraining cannot be attributed solely to convolution when the data recipe and model capacity differ. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:01e8a4dbfcbc] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:d61b3a2c0154] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:1381ace2c5eb]

For dense prediction, the original ViT's single-scale patch grid is a poor structural match for many CNN-era pipelines. PVT was motivated by this mismatch: unlike ViT, which the authors describe as designed mainly for classification and as having low-resolution outputs with high computational and memory cost at dense partitions, PVT builds a progressive shrinking pyramid and uses spatial-reduction attention. Its pyramid supplies multi-scale, higher-resolution features that can replace ResNet or ResNeXt backbones in frameworks such as RetinaNet and Mask R-CNN, while spatial-reduction attention lowers the cost of attention on larger feature maps. PVT is therefore not evidence that the original ViT already had a CNN-like pyramid; it is evidence that a later pure Transformer could adopt hierarchy to improve the dense-prediction interface. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:5e2261452395] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:b62e6b456bd6] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:2754995a3368] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:e107f162ef5e]

ViT-CoMer takes the complementary route of preserving the plain ViT branch while adding convolutional feature enhancement. Its authors identify two specific weaknesses of ViT for dense prediction: limited interaction among features inside patches and limited diversity of feature scales. The model injects spatial-pyramid, multi-receptive-field convolutional features and uses a CNN–Transformer bidirectional fusion module to combine hierarchical convolutional features with the ViT branch. A stated design reason for preserving the original ViT is compatibility with open-source pretrained ViT weights; vision-specific Transformers that alter the backbone may not directly load those weights. ViT-CoMer therefore demonstrates a hybrid remedy for plain ViT's dense-prediction weaknesses, but its results cannot be assigned to the original ViT alone because the added CNN branch and fusion modules change the mechanism. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:c41bdf05bdc3] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:80b3379c43b9] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:574bddc5a23a] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:0aecb65d2202]

CvT is another hybrid mechanism, but it changes the ViT block itself rather than attaching a separate pyramid branch. It introduces convolutional token embedding in a hierarchical multi-stage structure and replaces parts of the attention projection with convolutional projections in a convolutional Transformer block. The intended contribution is to combine CNN-like local translation, scale and distortion properties with Transformer-style dynamic attention and global context, while also allowing positional encoding to be removed in the reported model. CvT was evaluated on ImageNet-1k and after ImageNet-22k pretraining, with the paper reporting favorable accuracy relative to other Vision Transformers and ResNets at fewer parameters and lower FLOPs, and 87.7% top-1 accuracy for CvT-W24 after ImageNet-22k pretraining. These results support the hybrid design under its reported settings; they do not show that unchanged ViT and CNN backbones are equivalent. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:0:f6930946851d:claim:fd8c2f06a84a] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:4:6c76322fc1b3:claim:d61b3a2c0154] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:2928754fefd1]

CNN-inspired spatial reduction has also been imported into Transformers without adding a full convolutional branch. PiT starts from the original ViT and tests the CNN principle that spatial dimensions should decrease while channel dimensions increase with depth; its pooling-based architecture reports improved capability and generalization over ViT across classification, object detection and robustness experiments. HVT similarly pools visual tokens progressively to shorten the sequence, analogously to CNN feature-map downsampling, and reports that comparable-FLOP HVT models outperform competitive baselines on ImageNet and CIFAR-100; it also finds average-pooled visual tokens more discriminative than a single class token in its experiments. These methods show that hierarchy and token reduction are transferable design ideas, but they are modified Transformers rather than the original uniform-resolution ViT. [E:arxiv:2103.16302:abstract:claim:52d2ac897ca9] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:29e8b5535db7]

LeViT illustrates the separate objective of fast inference. It is a hybrid image-classification network that reuses Transformer attention but adopts CNN-inspired activation maps with decreasing resolutions and introduces attention bias for positional information. Its contribution is explicitly a speed–accuracy trade-off for high-speed inference across hardware measures rather than a redesign aimed primarily at dense-prediction heads. The paper reports that, around 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy, LeViT was five times faster than EfficientNet on CPU. That result must be tied to the measured hardware, model family and inference setting; it cannot be generalized into a universal latency advantage for Transformers over CNNs or for hybrids over both. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:a04e8d78ee90]

The unification literature further cautions against treating operator labels as completely disjoint categories. One line of work interprets vision Transformers as ConvNets with dynamic convolutions, placing existing Transformers and dynamic ConvNets in a common framework so that design choices can be compared side by side. The same perspective motivated replacing softmax in vision Transformers with common ConvNet components such as ReLU and Layer Normalization, and designing a depth-wise vision Transformer inspired by depth-wise convolution. This is an analytical and design-space connection: it explains how attention can resemble data-dependent, spatially global weighting, but it does not erase practical differences in parameter sharing, hierarchy, tokenization and the interfaces used by downstream heads. [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:2ca12e1e36c8] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:e7750f8d8f9a]

The applicability boundary of plain ViT is therefore narrower than its broad influence might suggest. It is directly applicable as a convolution-free patch-token encoder for image classification and transfer learning when large-scale pretraining is available, and its global attention creates representations that differ measurably from stagewise ResNets. It is less directly applicable as an unmodified drop-in backbone for RetinaNet-, Mask R-CNN- or feature-pyramid-style dense tasks because those systems benefit from multi-scale high-resolution maps and local feature interactions. PVT, CvT, PiT, HVT and ViT-CoMer address different parts of this mismatch through pyramids, convolution, pooling or fusion; each should be treated as a distinct adaptation with its own evidence rather than as proof that the original ViT possessed those properties. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:01e8a4dbfcbc] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:5e2261452395] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:b62e6b456bd6] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:0:f6930946851d:claim:fd8c2f06a84a] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:c41bdf05bdc3] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:80b3379c43b9] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:29e8b5535db7]

The applicability boundary of CNN backbones is also task- and recipe-dependent. Their local, hierarchical structure makes them natural feature extractors for classification and dense-prediction frameworks, and large supervised CNNs such as ConvNeXt were highly competitive across the broad BoB evaluation. Yet CNNs do not provide ViT's early, explicit all-pairs token mixing, and the CKA evidence indicates different internal representation propagation rather than merely a different implementation of the same computation. A CNN result obtained with one pretraining corpus, head and resolution cannot be directly compared with a ViT result obtained under another corpus or augmentation schedule. The methods-level conclusion is thus that architecture choice should be made jointly with pretraining scale, output hierarchy, task head, input resolution and measured efficiency, rather than by family name alone. ## Comparative Evidence Analysis

The experimental comparison should be read task by task rather than as one universal ranking. The original ViT paper's central classification claim was conditional: after pretraining on large data and transferring to ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and other recognition benchmarks, a pure patch-token Transformer attained excellent results compared with state-of-the-art convolutional networks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train. This supports ViT as a strong large-data classification backbone, but it does not make the result comparable to a CNN trained from scratch on a smaller corpus or to a CNN evaluated with a different resolution, head or pretraining schedule. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:01e8a4dbfcbc] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:83a29ddc89e9]

The strongest matched dense-prediction comparison in the selected evidence comes from PVT with RetinaNet on COCO val2017. Under the same detector family, PVT-Tiny with 23.0 million parameters reached 36.7% bounding-box AP versus ResNet-18 with 21.3 million parameters at 31.8% AP; PVT-Small with 34.2 million parameters reached 40.4% AP versus ResNet-50 with 37.7 million parameters at 36.3% AP, a 4.1-point absolute gap. At larger scale, PVT-Medium with 53.9 million parameters reached 41.9% AP versus ResNet-101 with 56.7 million parameters at 38.5% AP, and PVT-Large with 71.1 million parameters reached 42.6% AP versus ResNeXt-101-64x4d with 95.5 million parameters at 41.0% AP. The table also reports ViT-S/32 at 60.8 million parameters and 31.7% AP, indicating that the original single-scale ViT was not a competitive drop-in RetinaNet backbone in that setting. These comparisons share the COCO/RetinaNet interface, but PVT is a pyramid Transformer rather than the original ViT; therefore the result supports hierarchy and dense-feature design, not an unchanged-ViT advantage. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:1:452441575086:claim:ea0c6a09db7a] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:2754995a3368] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:b62e6b456bd6] PVT's reported advantage over the CNN baselines is specifically about dense-prediction feature interfaces. The authors argue that conventional CNN backbones expand their local receptive fields only with depth, whereas PVT provides a global receptive field through attention and a progressive shrinking pyramid for multi-scale, high-resolution features. The same paper distinguishes PVT from the original ViT by noting that ViT was designed mainly for classification, typically produces low-resolution single-scale outputs, and incurs high computation and memory cost on dense partitions. Thus the COCO numbers should not be summarized as “Transformers beat CNNs”: the controlled contrast is between pyramid Transformer backbones and ResNet/ResNeXt backbones under RetinaNet, while the original ViT result in the same table is a poor structural match. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:5e2261452395] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:b62e6b456bd6] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:e107f162ef5e] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:1:452441575086:claim:ea0c6a09db7a]

ViT-CoMer provides later evidence that adding convolutional multi-scale features can improve a plain ViT branch for dense tasks, but it is not a head-to-head test of original ViT versus a CNN. With advanced pretraining, ViT-CoMer-L achieved 64.3% AP on COCO val2017 without training on extra detection data such as Objects365, and 62.1% mIoU on ADE20K validation. The model's mechanism combines a preserved ViT branch with spatial-pyramid convolutional features, multi-receptive-field processing and CNN–Transformer bidirectional fusion. Because the reported numbers include those added modules and a specified advanced-pretraining recipe, they cannot be attributed to the original ViT alone or directly ranked against ResNet results obtained under different detectors, pretraining datasets or training schedules. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:3:547682e61b42:claim:574bddc5a23a] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:c41bdf05bdc3] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:80b3379c43b9] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:0aecb65d2202]

For broad backbone selection, Battle of the Backbones offers a different experimental regime: more than 1,500 training runs across classification, detection, out-of-distribution generalization and other tasks, with diverse architectures and pretraining methods. Its overall winners included supervised ConvNeXt-Base, SwinV2-Base trained using ImageNet-21k, and CLIP ViT-Base; at smaller scale, ConvNeXt-Tiny and SwinV2-Tiny were top performers, followed by DINO ViT-Small. The study reported that supervised convolutional networks performed best on most tasks among the models considered, but also found that this supervised advantage often reflected larger pretraining datasets and that self-supervised backbones were highly competitive in dataset-scale-matched comparisons. This is evidence about a broad portfolio of available pretrained backbones, not a controlled claim that convolution intrinsically outperforms the original ViT. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:7f5d1d9565aa] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:1381ace2c5eb] The BoB results also identify an interaction between architecture and pretraining scale. The paper reports that ViTs were more sensitive than CNNs to the amount of pretraining data and to the number of parameters. That finding is consistent with the original ViT premise that large-data pretraining is crucial, but it changes the interpretation of small-data or randomly initialized comparisons: a ViT and CNN with similar parameter counts are not necessarily operating under equally favorable inductive biases or pretraining conditions. Fair comparisons therefore need to report pretraining corpus size and supervision, initialization, parameter count, input resolution, augmentation and fine-tuning data; otherwise differences may reflect the training recipe rather than the backbone family. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:01e8a4dbfcbc] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:7f5d1d9565aa] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:1381ace2c5eb]

Representation experiments add a mechanistic dimension that accuracy tables do not capture. Using centered kernel alignment to compare layers in ViTs and ResNets on image-classification benchmarks, the analysis found that ViTs had a much more uniform, grid-like similarity structure, while ResNets separated more clearly into lower and higher stages. Cross-model CKA indicated that many lower ResNet layers were needed to become similar to roughly the lowest quarter of ViT layers, the upper half of ResNet corresponded approximately to the next third of ViT layers, and the final third of ViT was less similar to the examined ResNet layers. The authors linked the ViT pattern to early global aggregation by self-attention and strong feature propagation through residual connections. These are representation-structure findings, not accuracy rankings, and they do not establish which architecture is preferable under a fixed downstream budget. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:229fa6f9a60c] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:055b01c7c4c7] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:2a4fef07e3b5] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:d69956438fbf]

Hybrid and hierarchy-adapted models provide controlled design evidence, but their numbers should not be merged into a single original-ViT score. CvT introduced convolutional token embedding, a hierarchical stage structure and convolutional projections, and reported state-of-the-art ImageNet-1k performance relative to other Vision Transformers and ResNets with fewer parameters and lower FLOPs; after ImageNet-22k pretraining, CvT-W24 reached 87.7% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1k validation. PiT reported improved capability and generalization over ViT by adding CNN-inspired spatial pooling, and HVT reported that, at comparable FLOPs, progressively pooled hierarchical visual Transformers outperformed competitive baselines on ImageNet and CIFAR-100. These results support convolution-like hierarchy and token reduction as useful modifications, but they evaluate changed architectures and cannot be used as direct evidence that the original ViT beats CNN backbones. [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:0:f6930946851d:claim:fd8c2f06a84a] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:2928754fefd1] [E:arxiv:2103.16302:abstract:claim:52d2ac897ca9] [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:29e8b5535db7]

Efficiency comparisons are likewise setting-specific. LeViT, a hybrid fast-inference classifier using decreasing activation-map resolutions and attention bias, was reported to be about five times faster than EfficientNet on CPU around 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy. That speed claim is tied to the measured CPU inference setting and the particular LeViT–EfficientNet operating point; it does not imply a universal latency advantage for Transformers, CNNs or hybrids. Likewise, later edge-deployment work treats ViT inference latency and computational demand as deployment problems and uses model splitting and class-wise pruning, but its reported size and latency improvements concern an engineered deployment framework rather than a fair backbone-family benchmark. FLOPs, parameters, wall-clock latency, token count and memory therefore need to be kept as separate metrics. [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:a04e8d78ee90] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:e9de05afa6a2] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:3b258dca8f46] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:359b663e5dc3]

Taken together, the experiments support a conditional comparison rather than a winner by family label. The original ViT is strongly supported for large-scale pretrained image classification and transfer, and its global attention produces measurably different layer representations from ResNets. Conventional CNN backbones remain highly competitive, especially when supervised pretraining is large and when hierarchical feature maps are required; broad BoB testing found supervised CNNs best on most tasks in its model set. For detection and segmentation, the evidence favors hierarchical or hybrid adaptations—PVT, CvT or ViT-CoMer—over treating the original single-scale ViT as an unchanged CNN replacement. Cross-paper numbers such as ViT-CoMer's COCO/ADE20K results, CvT's ImageNet result and BoB's multi-task rankings are not directly rankable against one another unless task, head, pretraining, resolution, model scale and hardware are matched. ## Limitations and Open Problems

The first open problem is that the original ViT's strongest premise—large-scale pretraining—does not transfer automatically to every data regime. The original model was presented as a pure patch-token Transformer that performed very well after pretraining on large data and transfer to ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and other benchmarks. Battle of the Backbones later reported that ViTs were more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count. The practical implication is that a small-data, from-scratch comparison can confound architecture with data efficiency: ViT may lack the convolutional locality bias that helps CNNs under limited supervision, while a large-pretraining result may overstate ViT's readiness when comparable corpora are unavailable. This is a limitation of the evidence regime, not proof that either operator is intrinsically superior. [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:01e8a4dbfcbc] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:1381ace2c5eb] [E:arxiv:2010.11929:abstract:claim:83a29ddc89e9]

A second unresolved issue is how to obtain the benefits of early global attention without inheriting plain ViT's weak dense-prediction interface. The CKA study found that self-attention enabled early aggregation of global information and that ViT residual connections strongly propagated lower-layer features to higher layers; ViTs also showed more uniform representations across layers than stage-structured ResNets. Yet the same global-token design does not by itself supply the multi-scale, high-resolution feature maps used by common detection and segmentation systems. PVT and ViT-CoMer both identify plain ViT's single-scale representation as a dense-prediction limitation, and ViT-CoMer additionally points to limited interaction among local or inner-patch features. The open trade-off is therefore not simply global versus local processing, but how to preserve global context while producing the local detail and scale hierarchy that dense heads require. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:2a4fef07e3b5] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:d69956438fbf] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:5e2261452395] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:b62e6b456bd6] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:c41bdf05bdc3] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:80b3379c43b9]

Existing remedies illustrate the problem but do not produce one universally preferable backbone. PVT changes the architecture into a progressive shrinking pyramid with spatial-reduction attention so that it can replace ResNet or ResNeXt in dense pipelines; ViT-CoMer preserves a plain ViT branch but adds spatial-pyramid convolutional features and bidirectional CNN–Transformer fusion; CvT instead embeds convolution into token embedding and Transformer projections. These designs improve task fit through different structural changes, but their results cannot be interpreted as unchanged-ViT performance. A remaining challenge is to disentangle which gains come from global attention, local convolution, hierarchical scales, higher output resolution, or compatibility with a particular detection and segmentation head. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:5e2261452395] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:abstract:claim:b62e6b456bd6] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:c41bdf05bdc3] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:80b3379c43b9] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:0aecb65d2202] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:0:f6930946851d:claim:fd8c2f06a84a] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:abstract:claim:2928754fefd1]

Pretrained-weight compatibility creates another concrete constraint. ViT-CoMer's authors emphasize that preserving the original ViT allows the model to load powerful open-source ViT pretrained weights, whereas vision-specific Transformers that substantially alter the backbone may not directly reuse those weights. This means architectural improvements can carry a hidden cost: redesigning tokenization, stages, pooling or blocks may improve a target task but require new pretraining or reduce transfer from existing checkpoints. Conversely, retaining the original ViT to preserve checkpoint compatibility leaves its local-feature and single-scale weaknesses to be repaired by added modules. The field therefore lacks a free combination of unrestricted architecture redesign, immediate reuse of large-scale ViT pretraining, and simple dense-head integration. [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:96b1d3f20cf8] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:section:abstract:5:79491ce9b36b:claim:0aecb65d2202] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:c41bdf05bdc3] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:80b3379c43b9]

Representation differences also remain difficult to convert into actionable selection rules. CKA showed that ViT and ResNet internal representations were not organized identically: ViT layers were more uniformly similar, while ResNet representations divided more clearly into stages, and cross-model comparisons did not produce a simple one-to-one layer mapping. These findings help explain why ViT can preserve spatial information and aggregate globally, but they do not specify when that representation will improve accuracy, robustness, localization or efficiency under a fixed budget. A practical open problem is therefore to connect representation-structure measurements to downstream decisions rather than treating uniform features, stagewise features or early global aggregation as automatically beneficial. [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:229fa6f9a60c] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:055b01c7c4c7] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:2a4fef07e3b5] [E:arxiv:2108.08810:section:4_representation_structure_of_vits_and_convolutional_networks:0:a15b8fa3bc59:claim:d69956438fbf]

Efficiency remains multidimensional and cannot be settled by parameters, FLOPs or architecture family alone. Plain ViT attention operates over a token sequence whose cost is sensitive to image resolution and token count; PVT explicitly uses spatial-reduction attention because learning high-resolution features with Transformer tokens is resource-intensive, and later edge work describes ViT computational demand and inference latency as barriers on resource-constrained devices. CNNs are not uniformly cheaper, however: their cost also changes with width, depth, resolution and stage design. LeViT's reported five-fold CPU speed advantage over EfficientNet near 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy is tied to its hybrid design, hardware and operating point. The unresolved requirement is to report token count, memory, wall-clock latency, hardware, resolution and accuracy together rather than inferring deployment efficiency from one proxy. [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:5e2261452395] [E:arxiv:2102.12122:section:abstract:3:4ed8cc57457f:claim:e107f162ef5e] [E:arxiv:2104.01136:abstract:claim:a04e8d78ee90] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:e9de05afa6a2] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:3b258dca8f46] [E:arxiv:2410.11650:abstract:claim:359b663e5dc3]

Hierarchical token reduction is useful but introduces its own trade-offs. HVT progressively pools visual tokens to shorten the sequence and reduce computational cost, analogous to CNN downsampling, while PiT tests the CNN principle of decreasing spatial dimensions and increasing channels with depth. Such pooling can improve scalability and classification results, but it may discard fine spatial detail that matters for localization, segmentation or high-resolution recognition. The selected studies support pooling and spatial-dimension conversion as effective design choices in their reported experiments, but they do not resolve how aggressively tokens should be merged across tasks. Thus, token compression is both a remedy for attention cost and a potential source of information loss. [E:arxiv:2103.10619:abstract:claim:29e8b5535db7] [E:arxiv:2103.16302:abstract:claim:52d2ac897ca9]

Broad benchmarking further shows that backbone choice cannot be isolated from pretraining supervision and corpus scale. Battle of the Backbones found that supervised convolutional networks performed best on most tasks among the models it considered, while also reporting that self-supervised backbones were highly competitive when pretraining dataset scale was matched. Its winners included supervised ConvNeXt-Base, ImageNet-21k-trained SwinV2-Base and CLIP ViT-Base, demonstrating that architecture, objective and data source interact. The open problem is fair comparison: two backbones with the same parameter count can differ in pretraining corpus, supervision type, augmentation, tokenizer or resolution, so an observed win may not identify the causal architectural component. Future comparisons need matched data and compute as well as multiple downstream tasks. [E:arxiv:2310.19909:abstract:claim:7f5d1d9565aa] [E:arxiv:2310.19909:section:1_1_battle_of_the_backbones_the_tldr:0:34343181f775:claim:1381ace2c5eb]

The apparent CNN–Transformer boundary is also less sharp than early comparisons suggest. Work interpreting vision Transformers as ConvNets with dynamic convolutions places the families in a shared design space and shows that some Transformer components can be replaced or redesigned using ConvNet-inspired choices. Hybrid models such as CvT and ViT-CoMer likewise combine local convolution with global attention. This convergence is useful for design, but it complicates claims about a pure family advantage: once a model includes convolutional token embedding, pyramidal pooling, convolutional branches or dynamic-convolution-like attention, its evidence no longer isolates the original ViT or a conventional CNN. A remaining challenge is to evaluate components under controlled ablations while retaining realistic pretraining and downstream settings. [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:2ca12e1e36c8] [E:arxiv:2309.10713:abstract:claim:e7750f8d8f9a] [E:arxiv:2103.15808:section:abstract:0:f6930946851d:claim:fd8c2f06a84a] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:c41bdf05bdc3] [E:arxiv:2403.07392:abstract:claim:80b3379c43b9]

Finally, the evidence base is strongest for 2D image classification and selected dense-prediction benchmarks, leaving deployment- and domain-specific questions unresolved. The original ViT evidence centers on image recognition transfer, PVT and ViT-CoMer emphasize COCO- and ADE20K-style detection or segmentation, and BoB covers a broad but still defined suite of tasks. Those results should not be generalized automatically to video, 3D vision, medical imaging, OCR, arbitrary high-resolution multimodal inputs or extreme edge environments without separate evidence. The main implication is that backbone selection should remain conditional: match the model's locality and global-context mechanism, feature hierarchy, pretraining recipe, output interface and measured efficiency to the task, rather than choosing a universal winner between the original ViT and CNN backbones. ## Conclusion

The central answer is that original ViT and CNN backbones embody different trade-offs. Plain ViT is a strong large-data classification and transfer backbone whose global token mixing creates representations distinct from stagewise ResNets, but its original evidence should not be generalized to small-data training from scratch or to unmodified use in CNN-era dense-prediction pipelines. Conventional CNNs remain competitive and structurally convenient where locality, staged scales and high-resolution feature maps matter. For detection and segmentation, the supported choice is not “Transformer” or “CNN” by family label: PVT's pyramid, CvT's convolutional Transformer blocks, ViT-CoMer's CNN–Transformer fusion, and pooling models such as PiT and HVT are adaptations that change the original ViT mechanism. Their gains cannot be assigned to plain ViT, just as ConvNeXt or ResNet results under one pretraining recipe cannot be assigned to convolution alone. A defensible comparison must match task head, feature hierarchy, resolution, parameter scale, pretraining corpus, supervision, compute and measured hardware efficiency. The main trade-off is therefore global context versus built-in locality and scale hierarchy, mediated by data and deployment regime. ViT offers early global aggregation but depends strongly on large pretraining and has a poor native dense-head interface; CNNs offer inductive locality and multi-scale maps but not ViT's explicit early all-pairs token mixing. No reviewed evidence establishes a universal backbone winner; selection should follow the downstream interface, available pretraining and task-specific efficiency measurements.
