assertions.source_quote: Hybrid and hierarchy-adapted models provide controlled design evidence, but their numbers should not be merged into a single original-ViT score. CvT introduced convolutional token embedding, a hierarchical stage structure and convolutional projections, and reported state-of-the-art ImageNet-1k performance relative to other Vision Transformers and ResNets with fewer parameters and lower FLOPs; after ImageNet-22k pretraining, CvT-W24 reached 87.7% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1k validation. PiT reported improved capability and generalization over ViT by adding CNN-inspired spatial pooling, and HVT reported that, at comparable FLOPs, progressively pooled hierarchical visual Transformers outperformed competitive baselines on ImageNet and CIFAR-100. These results support convolution-like hierarchy and token reduction as useful modifications, but they evaluate changed architectures and cannot be used as direct evidence that the original ViT beats CNN backbones. assertions.source_quote: Efficiency comparisons are likewise setting-specific. LeViT, a hybrid fast-inference classifier using decreasing activation-map resolutions and attention bias, was reported to be about five times faster than EfficientNet on CPU around 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy. That speed claim is tied to the measured CPU inference setting and the particular LeViT–EfficientNet operating point; it does not imply a universal latency advantage for Transformers, CNNs or hybrids. Likewise, later edge-deployment work treats ViT inference latency and computational demand as deployment problems and uses model splitting and class-wise pruning, but its reported size and latency improvements concern an engineered deployment framework rather than a fair backbone-family benchmark. FLOPs, parameters, wall-clock latency, token count and memory therefore need to be kept as separate metrics. assertions.source_quote: Taken together, the experiments support a conditional comparison rather than a winner by family label. The original ViT is strongly supported for large-scale pretrained image classification and transfer, and its global attention produces measurably different layer representations from ResNets. Conventional CNN backbones remain highly competitive, especially when supervised pretraining is large and when hierarchical feature maps are required; broad BoB testing found supervised CNNs best on most tasks in its model set. For detection and segmentation, the evidence favors hierarchical or hybrid adaptations—PVT, CvT or ViT-CoMer—over treating the original single-scale ViT as an unchanged CNN replacement. Cross-paper numbers such as ViT-CoMer's COCO/ADE20K results, CvT's ImageNet result and BoB's multi-task rankings are not directly rankable against one another unless task, head, pretraining, resolution, model scale and hardware are matched. assertions.source_quote: The first open problem is that the original ViT's strongest premise—large-scale pretraining—does not transfer automatically to every data regime. The original model was presented as a pure patch-token Transformer that performed very well after pretraining on large data and transfer to ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB and other benchmarks. Battle of the Backbones later reported that ViTs were more sensitive than CNNs to pretraining-data amount and parameter count. The practical implication is that a small-data, from-scratch comparison can confound architecture with data efficiency: ViT may lack the convolutional locality bias that helps CNNs under limited supervision, while a large-pretraining result may overstate ViT's readiness when comparable corpora are unavailable. This is a limitation of the evidence regime, not proof that either operator is intrinsically superior. assertions.source_quote: A second unresolved issue is how to obtain the benefits of early global attention without inheriting plain ViT's weak dense-prediction interface. The CKA study found that self-attention enabled early aggregation of global information and that ViT residual connections strongly propagated lower-layer features to higher layers; ViTs also showed more uniform representations across layers than stage-structured ResNets. Yet the same global-token design does not by itself supply the multi-scale, high-resolution feature maps used by common detection and segmentation systems. PVT and ViT-CoMer both identify plain ViT's single-scale representation as a dense-prediction limitation, and ViT-CoMer additionally points to limited interaction among local or inner-patch features. The open trade-off is therefore not simply global versus local processing, but how to preserve global context while producing the local detail and scale hierarchy that dense heads require. assertions.source_quote: Existing remedies illustrate the problem but do not produce one universally preferable backbone. PVT changes the architecture into a progressive shrinking pyramid with spatial-reduction attention so that it can replace ResNet or ResNeXt in dense pipelines; ViT-CoMer preserves a plain ViT branch but adds spatial-pyramid convolutional features and bidirectional CNN–Transformer fusion; CvT instead embeds convolution into token embedding and Transformer projections. assertions.source_quote: Pretrained-weight compatibility creates another concrete constraint. ViT-CoMer's authors emphasize that preserving the original ViT allows the model to load powerful open-source ViT pretrained weights, whereas vision-specific Transformers that substantially alter the backbone may not directly reuse those weights. This means architectural improvements can carry a hidden cost: redesigning tokenization, stages, pooling or blocks may improve a target task but require new pretraining or reduce transfer from existing checkpoints. Conversely, retaining the original ViT to preserve checkpoint compatibility leaves its local-feature and single-scale weaknesses to be repaired by added modules. The field therefore lacks a free combination of unrestricted architecture redesign, immediate reuse of large-scale ViT pretraining, and simple dense-head integration. assertions.source_quote: Representation differences also remain difficult to convert into actionable selection rules. CKA showed that ViT and ResNet internal representations were not organized identically: ViT layers were more uniformly similar, while ResNet representations divided more clearly into stages, and cross-model comparisons did not produce a simple one-to-one layer mapping. These findings help explain why ViT can preserve spatial information and aggregate globally, but they do not specify when that representation will improve accuracy, robustness, localization or efficiency under a fixed budget. A practical open problem is therefore to connect representation-structure measurements to downstream decisions rather than treating uniform features, stagewise features or early global aggregation as automatically beneficial. assertions.source_quote: Efficiency remains multidimensional and cannot be settled by parameters, FLOPs or architecture family alone. Plain ViT attention operates over a token sequence whose cost is sensitive to image resolution and token count; PVT explicitly uses spatial-reduction attention because learning high-resolution features with Transformer tokens is resource-intensive, and later edge work describes ViT computational demand and inference latency as barriers on resource-constrained devices. CNNs are not uniformly cheaper, however: their cost also changes with width, depth, resolution and stage design. LeViT's reported five-fold CPU speed advantage over EfficientNet near 80% ImageNet top-1 accuracy is tied to its hybrid design, hardware and operating point. The unresolved requirement is to report token count, memory, wall-clock latency, hardware, resolution and accuracy together rather than inferring deployment efficiency from one proxy. assertions.source_quote: Hierarchical token reduction is useful but introduces its own trade-offs. HVT progressively pools visual tokens to shorten the sequence and reduce computational cost, analogous to CNN downsampling, while PiT tests the CNN principle of decreasing spatial dimensions and increasing channels with depth. Such pooling can improve scalability and classification results, but it may discard fine spatial detail that matters for localization, segmentation or high-resolution recognition. The selected studies support pooling and spatial-dimension conversion as effective design choices in their reported experiments, but they do not resolve how aggressively tokens should be merged across tasks. Thus, token compression is both a remedy for attention cost and a potential source of information loss. assertions.source_quote: Broad benchmarking further shows that backbone choice cannot be isolated from pretraining supervision and corpus scale. Battle of the Backbones found that supervised convolutional networks performed best on most tasks among the models it considered, while also reporting that self-supervised backbones were highly competitive when pretraining dataset scale was matched. Its winners included supervised ConvNeXt-Base, ImageNet-21k-trained SwinV2-Base and CLIP ViT-Base, demonstrating that architecture, objective and data source interact. The open problem is fair comparison: two backbones with the same parameter count can differ in pretraining corpus, supervision type or input resolution, so an observed win may not identify the causal architectural component. Future comparisons need matched data and compute as well as multiple downstream tasks. assertions.source_quote: Broad benchmarking further shows that backbone choice cannot be isolated from pretraining supervision and corpus scale. Battle of the Backbones found that supervised convolutional networks performed best on most tasks among the models it considered, while also reporting that self-supervised backbones were highly competitive when pretraining dataset scale was matched. Its winners included supervised ConvNeXt-Base, ImageNet-21k-trained SwinV2-Base and CLIP ViT-Base, demonstrating that architecture, objective and data source interact. The open problem is fair comparison: two backbones with the same parameter count can differ in pretraining corpus, supervision type or input resolution, so an observed win may not identify the causal architectural component. Future comparisons need matched data and compute as well as multiple downstream tasks. assertions.source_quote: The apparent CNN–Transformer boundary is also less sharp than early comparisons suggest. Work interpreting vision Transformers as ConvNets with dynamic convolutions places the families in a shared design space and shows that some Transformer components can be replaced or redesigned using ConvNet-inspired choices. Hybrid models such as CvT and ViT-CoMer likewise combine local convolution with global attention. This convergence is useful for design, but it complicates claims about a pure family advantage: once a model includes convolutional token embedding, pyramidal pooling, convolutional branches or dynamic-convolution-like attention, its evidence no longer isolates the original ViT or a conventional CNN. A remaining challenge is to evaluate components under controlled ablations while retaining realistic pretraining and downstream settings. assertions.source_quote: Finally, the evidence base is strongest for 2D image classification and selected dense-prediction benchmarks, leaving deployment- and domain-specific questions unresolved. The original ViT evidence centers on image recognition transfer, PVT and ViT-CoMer emphasize COCO- and ADE20K-style detection or segmentation, and BoB covers a broad but still defined suite of tasks. Those results should not be generalized automatically to video, 3D vision, medical imaging, OCR, arbitrary high-resolution multimodal inputs or extreme edge environments without separate evidence. The main implication is that backbone selection should remain conditional: match the model's locality and global-context mechanism, feature hierarchy, pretraining recipe, output interface and measured efficiency to the task, rather than choosing a universal winner between the original ViT and CNN backbones.
